by_task.when: An asset factually matches an exemption category, but the statute states a dollar ceiling or limits the exemption to one item.
by_task.procedure: For EC, treat the ceiling as limiting protected value rather than citation eligibility. Evaluate every matching asset independently and include the category citation for each candidate; do not make a final portfolio choice among multiple matching assets. Retain any independently applicable general-property citation as well.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not cite the category when its factual type, use, ownership, or other nonmonetary condition is absent. This instruction does not determine the protected amount for EV.

by_task.when: Considering 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3) for personal-use property.
by_task.procedure: Include § 522(d)(3) only when the asset is one of its listed categories: household furnishings or goods, apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments. Personal use alone does not place an unlisted item in this paragraph.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify a firearm as § 522(d)(3) property merely because it is personally or household used; another independently applicable exemption, including § 522(d)(5), is unaffected.

by_task.when: Federal § 522(d) exemptions are authorized and an asset may be household furnishings or goods, apparel, an appliance, a book, an animal, a crop, or a musical instrument.
by_task.procedure: Include § 522(d)(3) only for a listed category. For the whole item, report its actual value when below $700 and otherwise report $700; the ceiling is not the claim value by itself. Assess § 522(d)(5) separately.
by_task.avoid_when: Personal use alone is insufficient. Firearms and jewelry are not § 522(d)(3) categories; assess jewelry under § 522(d)(4) and firearms only under other applicable alternatives.

by_task.when: The public solved steps authorize federal § 522(d) exemptions and the asset is property of the debtor's estate.
by_task.procedure: Independently include 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) for the asset. It applies to any property and has a base amount in addition to any unused homestead amount, so do not require the asset to lack a specific exemption or require proof of unused homestead value. Keep every applicable specific § 522(d) citation too.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not include § 522(d)(5) when federal § 522(d) exemptions are unavailable under the supplied solved steps or the asset is not debtor property.

by_task.when: The solved steps authorize federal § 522(d) exemptions and the asset is property of one or more debtors.
by_task.procedure: For every such asset, include § 522(d)(5) as a separate alternative even when a specific federal exemption also applies. Do not subtract another exemption reported for the same asset. Unless the supplied facts establish that homestead value was consumed elsewhere, use a $15,425 ceiling for each debtor; apply it to that debtor's interest, add the protected interests, and report no more than the whole asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 522(d)(5) because the asset has a specific exemption or is worth less than the ceiling. Exclude it only when federal exemptions are unavailable or the asset is not debtor property.

by_task.when: Considering 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(a) for an Illinois personal asset.
by_task.procedure: Use paragraph (a) for necessary wearing apparel, Bibles, school books, or family pictures. Determine whether the asset is actually within one of those listed classes; being worn or used as adornment is not enough.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat ordinary jewelry as necessary wearing apparel. Its possible § 12-1001(b) alternative must be assessed independently.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and the asset may be necessary wearing apparel, a Bible, a school book, or a family picture.
by_task.procedure: Include § 12-1001(a) only for a listed class and report the whole asset value because this paragraph states no dollar ceiling. Assess § 12-1001(b) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat ordinary jewelry or personal adornment as necessary wearing apparel.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and the debtor owns personal property used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure: Include 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) as an independent other-property alternative, including when the same asset also qualifies as apparel, a motor vehicle, or a prescribed health aid. Retain each applicable specific citation.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 12-1001(b) to real property, nondebtor property, or property used for business rather than personal purposes.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and one or more debtors own personal property used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure: Check § 12-1001(b) for every personal-property asset, including apparel, motor vehicles, prescribed health aids, and objects that resemble tools. Apply $4,000 to each debtor's equity interest, add the protected interests, and cap the result at the whole asset value. Keep every independently applicable specific citation.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not infer business use merely from an object's type; use the task's personal-use default unless facts expressly establish business use. Do not apply paragraph (b) to real property, nondebtor property, or expressly business-use property.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are authorized and the asset is personal property in which the debtor has an interest.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative, even when the asset also fits a named Oregon category or exceeds the paragraph's protected-value ceiling. Retain all applicable named-category citations.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply paragraph (p) to real property, property lacking a debtor interest, or a context where Oregon law is unavailable.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are authorized and the asset is personal property in which a debtor has an interest.
by_task.procedure: Perform this check for every personal-property asset: include § 18.345(1)(p) independently for firearms, vehicles, jewelry, apparel, household goods, and other personal property even when a named Oregon exemption applies. Report the lesser of the whole asset value and $400, and retain every named-category alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit paragraph (p) because a specific Oregon paragraph applies or because the asset exceeds $400. Do not apply it to real property, property lacking a debtor interest, or when Oregon law is unavailable.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are authorized and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general monetary exemption for the asset, alongside every applicable particular-property exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 8123 to property that is not the debtor's or when Pennsylvania law is not an allowable namespace.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are authorized and the asset is property of one or more judgment debtors.
by_task.procedure: For every debtor-owned asset, include § 8123 independently of any particular-property exemption. Protect the lesser of $300 and each debtor's interest, add those protected interests, and cap the result at the whole asset value. Thus a sole debtor cannot exceed $300, while two equal debtor-spouses may reach $600 only when the asset is worth at least $600.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because another Pennsylvania exemption applies, and do not report a ceiling greater than the whole asset value. Exclude it only for nondebtor property or when Pennsylvania law is unavailable.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are authorized and § 33-1125(1) is being considered for a personal asset.
by_task.procedure: Include § 33-1125(1) only for actual wearing apparel, with the lesser of its value and $500. Test any separately listed ring or watch provision on its own terms.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify an ordinary pendant, bracelet, or other jewelry as wearing apparel merely because it is worn.

by_task.when: Federal § 522(d) exemptions are authorized and the asset is jewelry held primarily for personal, family, or household use.
by_task.procedure: Include § 522(d)(4) and report the lesser of the whole jewelry item's value and $1,875. Assess § 522(d)(5) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry under § 522(d)(3), and do not apply § 522(d)(4) to nonjewelry property or property lacking the required use.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and the debtor owns a motor vehicle used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure: Include § 12-1001(c) with the lesser of the whole vehicle value and $2,400. Calculate the independent § 12-1001(b) alternative under its own equity ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute paragraph (b)'s $4,000 ceiling for paragraph (c), and do not double paragraph (c)'s ceiling merely because two debtors jointly own the vehicle.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and § 12-1001(d) is being considered for an implement, professional book, or tool.
by_task.procedure: Include § 12-1001(d) only when facts establish that the property is used in the debtor's trade, and report no more than the applicable $1,500 ceiling. For personally used property, assess § 12-1001(b) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not infer trade use from the object's name or capability; under the task's personal-use default, absent express trade facts do not apply paragraph (d).

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are authorized and the asset is wearing apparel or jewelry.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(b). Apply the $1,800 ceiling to each qualifying debtor interest as allowed by § 18.345(3), combine protected interests for jointly owned property, and never exceed the whole asset value. Assess paragraph (p) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the vehicle or household-goods paragraph, and do not omit paragraph (b) merely because paragraph (p) also applies.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are authorized and the asset is a household good, furniture, radio, television, or utensil held primarily for personal, family, or household use.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(f) and report the lesser of the whole asset value and $3,000. Assess § 18.345(1)(p) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit paragraph (f) because paragraph (p) applies, and do not use paragraph (f) for property lacking the required household character or use.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are authorized and the asset is an occupied homestead of one or more debtor household members.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are authorized and § 8124(a)(1) is being considered for personal property.

by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply the wearing-apparel paragraph to firearms, jewelry, or other property merely because no more specific Pennsylvania paragraph is available.

by_task.when: Wisconsin exemptions are authorized and tangible personal property is held primarily for personal, family, or household use under § 815.18(3)(d).

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and § 12-1001(d) is being considered for an implement, professional book, or tool.
by_task.procedure: Include § 12-1001(d) only when facts establish that the property is used in the debtor's trade, and report no more than the applicable $1,500 ceiling. For personally used property, assess § 12-1001(b) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not infer trade use from the object's name or capability; under the task's personal-use default, absent express trade facts do not apply paragraph (d).

operations.rationale: The parent inferred trade use from a tool-like description despite the supplied personal-use default, producing an extra paragraph (d) claim and omitting paragraph (b).

diagnoses.rule_anchor: Include § 522(d)(5) independently of every specific federal exemption.
Include § 522(d)(3) only for a listed category and report the lesser of the whole item's value and the $700 per-item ceiling. Assess § 522(d)(5) separately.

Protect up to $300 of each spouse's interest and report the sum for the whole asset without exceeding its value; thus one debtor has a $300 ceiling and two debtor-spouses can have a $600 whole-asset ceiling.
Include § 18.345(1)(p) independently even when a named Oregon exemption also applies.
Include § 12-1001(b) independently, including for apparel, motor vehicles, and prescribed health aids.

by_task.when: An asset factually matches an exemption category, but the statute states a dollar ceiling or limits the exemption to one item.
by_task.procedure: For EC, treat the ceiling as limiting protected value rather than citation eligibility. Evaluate every matching asset independently and include the category citation for each candidate; do not make a final portfolio choice among multiple matching assets. Retain any independently applicable general-property citation as well.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not cite the category when its factual type, use, ownership, or other nonmonetary condition is absent. This instruction does not determine the protected amount for EV.

by_task.when: The public solved steps authorize federal § 522(d) exemptions and the asset is property of the debtor's estate.
by_task.procedure: Independently include 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) for the asset. It applies to any property and has a base amount in addition to any unused homestead amount, so do not require the asset to lack a specific exemption or require proof of unused homestead value. Keep every applicable specific § 522(d) citation too.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not include § 522(d)(5) when federal § 522(d) exemptions are unavailable under the supplied solved steps or the asset is not debtor property.

by_task.when: The solved steps authorize federal § 522(d) exemptions and the asset is property of one or more debtors.
by_task.procedure: For every such asset, include § 522(d)(5) as a separate alternative even when a specific federal exemption also applies. Do not subtract another exemption reported for the same asset. Unless the supplied facts establish that homestead value was consumed elsewhere, use a $15,425 ceiling for each debtor; apply it to that debtor's interest, add the protected interests, and report no more than the whole asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 522(d)(5) because the asset has a specific exemption or is worth less than the ceiling. Exclude it only when federal exemptions are unavailable or the asset is not debtor property.

by_task.when: Considering 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3) for personal-use property.
by_task.procedure: Include § 522(d)(3) only when the asset is one of its listed categories: household furnishings or goods, apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments. Personal use alone does not place an unlisted item in this paragraph.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify a firearm as § 522(d)(3) property merely because it is personally or household used; another independently applicable exemption, including § 522(d)(5), is unaffected.

by_task.when: Federal § 522(d) exemptions are authorized and an asset may be household furnishings or goods, apparel, an appliance, a book, an animal, a crop, or a musical instrument.
by_task.procedure: Include § 522(d)(3) only for a listed category. For the whole item, report its actual value when below $700 and otherwise report $700; the ceiling is not the claim value by itself. Assess § 522(d)(5) separately.
by_task.avoid_when: Personal use alone is insufficient. Firearms and jewelry are not § 522(d)(3) categories; assess jewelry under § 522(d)(4) and firearms only under other applicable alternatives.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are authorized and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general monetary exemption for the asset, alongside every applicable particular-property exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 8123 to property that is not the debtor's or when Pennsylvania law is not an allowable namespace.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are authorized and the asset is property of one or more judgment debtors.
by_task.procedure: For every debtor-owned asset, include § 8123 independently of any particular-property exemption. Protect the lesser of $300 and each debtor's interest, add those protected interests, and cap the result at the whole asset value. Thus a sole debtor cannot exceed $300, while two equal debtor-spouses may reach $600 only when the asset is worth at least $600.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because another Pennsylvania exemption applies, and do not report a ceiling greater than the whole asset value. Exclude it only for nondebtor property or when Pennsylvania law is unavailable.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are authorized and the asset is personal property in which the debtor has an interest.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative, even when the asset also fits a named Oregon category or exceeds the paragraph's protected-value ceiling. Retain all applicable named-category citations.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply paragraph (p) to real property, property lacking a debtor interest, or a context where Oregon law is unavailable.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are authorized and the asset is personal property in which a debtor has an interest.
by_task.procedure: Perform this check for every personal-property asset: include § 18.345(1)(p) independently for firearms, vehicles, jewelry, apparel, household goods, and other personal property even when a named Oregon exemption applies. Report the lesser of the whole asset value and $400, and retain every named-category alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit paragraph (p) because a specific Oregon paragraph applies or because the asset exceeds $400. Do not apply it to real property, property lacking a debtor interest, or when Oregon law is unavailable.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and the debtor owns personal property used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure: Include 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) as an independent other-property alternative, including when the same asset also qualifies as apparel, a motor vehicle, or a prescribed health aid. Retain each applicable specific citation.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 12-1001(b) to real property, nondebtor property, or property used for business rather than personal purposes.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and one or more debtors own personal property used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure: Check § 12-1001(b) for every personal-property asset, including apparel, motor vehicles, prescribed health aids, and objects that resemble tools. Apply $4,000 to each debtor's equity interest, add the protected interests, and cap the result at the whole asset value. Keep every independently applicable specific citation.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not infer business use merely from an object's type; use the task's personal-use default unless facts expressly establish business use. Do not apply paragraph (b) to real property, nondebtor property, or expressly business-use property.

by_task.when: Considering 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(a) for an Illinois personal asset.
by_task.procedure: Use paragraph (a) for necessary wearing apparel, Bibles, school books, or family pictures. Determine whether the asset is actually within one of those listed classes; being worn or used as adornment is not enough.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat ordinary jewelry as necessary wearing apparel. Its possible § 12-1001(b) alternative must be assessed independently.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and the asset may be necessary wearing apparel, a Bible, a school book, or a family picture.
by_task.procedure: Include § 12-1001(a) only for a listed class and report the whole asset value because this paragraph states no dollar ceiling. Assess § 12-1001(b) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat ordinary jewelry or personal adornment as necessary wearing apparel.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and the debtor owns a motor vehicle used for personal rather than business purposes.
by_task.procedure: Include § 12-1001(c) with the lesser of the whole vehicle value and $2,400. Calculate the independent § 12-1001(b) alternative under its own equity ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute paragraph (b)'s $4,000 ceiling for paragraph (c), and do not double paragraph (c)'s ceiling merely because two debtors jointly own the vehicle.

by_task.when: Wisconsin exemptions are authorized and tangible personal property is held primarily for personal, family, or household use under § 815.18(3)(d).
by_task.procedure: Include § 815.18(3)(d) and report the lesser of the whole asset value and the applicable $12,000 ceiling. The ceiling limits protection; it is not automatically the claim_value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use paragraph (d) for property lacking the required personal, family, or household use, and do not report $12,000 for an asset worth less.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are authorized and § 33-1125(1) is being considered for a personal asset.
by_task.procedure: Include § 33-1125(1) only for actual wearing apparel, with the lesser of its value and $500. Test any separately listed ring or watch provision on its own terms.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify an ordinary pendant, bracelet, or other jewelry as wearing apparel merely because it is worn.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are authorized and § 8124(a)(1) is being considered for personal property.
by_task.procedure: Include § 8124(a)(1) only for wearing apparel and report the whole apparel value because the paragraph states no dollar ceiling. Assess § 8123 independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply the wearing-apparel paragraph to firearms, jewelry, or other property merely because no more specific Pennsylvania paragraph is available.

by_task.when: Federal § 522(d) exemptions are authorized and the asset is jewelry held primarily for personal, family, or household use.
by_task.procedure: Include § 522(d)(4) and report the lesser of the whole jewelry item's value and $1,875. Assess § 522(d)(5) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry under § 522(d)(3), and do not apply § 522(d)(4) to nonjewelry property or property lacking the required use.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are authorized and the asset is a professionally prescribed prosthetic or physician-authorized respiratory or mobility aid.
by_task.procedure: Include Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(9) and report the whole asset value because that paragraph states no dollar ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the household-furnishings exemption merely because the medical equipment is used at home; require professional prescription or authorization.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are authorized and § 33-1125(4) is being considered for a ring.
by_task.procedure: Include § 33-1125(4) only when facts identify an engagement ring or wedding ring, and report the lesser of its value and $2,000.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not extend the paragraph to anniversary, decorative, or other rings merely because they are jewelry.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are authorized and the asset is a household good, furniture, radio, television, or utensil held primarily for personal, family, or household use.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(f) and report the lesser of the whole asset value and $3,000. Assess § 18.345(1)(p) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit paragraph (f) because paragraph (p) applies, and do not use paragraph (f) for property lacking the required household character or use.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are authorized and the asset is wearing apparel or jewelry.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(b). Apply the $1,800 ceiling to each qualifying debtor interest as allowed by § 18.345(3), combine protected interests for jointly owned property, and never exceed the whole asset value. Assess paragraph (p) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the vehicle or household-goods paragraph, and do not omit paragraph (b) merely because paragraph (p) also applies.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are authorized and the asset is an occupied homestead of one or more debtor household members.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.395(1). Report up to $40,000 for one debtor, but when two or more household members are debtors with interests subject to execution, report the lesser of the whole homestead value and their $50,000 combined ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use $40,000 as the final ceiling for a qualifying multi-debtor household, and do not apply the homestead paragraph without the required abode and occupancy facts.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are authorized and § 12-1001(d) is being considered for an implement, professional book, or tool.
by_task.procedure: Include § 12-1001(d) only when facts establish that the property is used in the debtor's trade, and report no more than the applicable $1,500 ceiling. For personally used property, assess § 12-1001(b) independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not infer trade use from the object's name or capability; under the task's personal-use default, absent express trade facts do not apply paragraph (d).
